notes:
**Research notes: 1 Chronicles 29**

These notes rely mostly on older commentaries collected on biblehub.com and studylight.org, plus Enduring Word, Precept Austin and two OCA pages. I couldn't find anything on these verses from the denominational sites (desiringgod, gty, ligonier, seedbed, lcms and the others), from bibleodyssey or netbible study notes, from newadvent or catholic.com, or from prosperity or word of faith teachers. Those areas are left out below.

---

**v. 1**
- The pressure David felt about Solomon's youth repeats 1 Chr 22:5. The words "whom alone God hath chosen" may protect David against charges of favouritism from his older sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Benson: David urges the assembly to help Solomon, because God chose him but he is still a youth who needs their support. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-1.htm
- Gill: the "great work" means both ruling and, above all, building the temple. The Targum reads "for the Word of the Lord God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Guzik: the work was great because it was for God. It needed more resources than a young king could gather alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Older and modern scholarship: "palace" (birah) is probably a Persian loanword, used elsewhere for the Persian royal residence. The Expositor's Bible calls putting it in David's mouth an anachronism, like "darics" in v. 7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-1.htm; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-chronicles-29.html

**v. 2**
- Matthew Henry: "with all my might" means David made the temple his business. Work for God must be done with all our might. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_029.cfm
- Pulpit gives word notes on the six kinds of stone. The word for "stones to be set" is also used for a priest's installation (Lev 8:33). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Gill: it is hard to say what the stones were for, but they were certainly used to decorate the house (2 Chr 3:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: the word for "personal treasure" (segullah) is the same one used for Israel as God's "special treasure" (Ex 19:5). It carries the sense of affection for one's own possession. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Guzik: David gave because he loved God's house (Matt 6:21). He gave "over and above" what he had already prepared. "My God" shows a personal tie. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: the amounts are uncertain, and so is the location of Ophir (Arabia and India are both proposed). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- The Ryrie Study Bible, quoted by Precept Austin, puts the gold at about 3.6 million ounces and the silver at about 8.4 million ounces. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64119/
- Gill cites Prideaux, who thought David could give this much only because of trade with Ophir. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 5**
- Payne, quoted by Guzik: "consecrate himself" is literally "fill his hand," a phrase used for ordaining priests. Scripture puts giving on that same level of devotion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Guzik: David hardly needed the people's gifts. He gave them the chance to give for their own sake. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Pulpit: the appeal is about practical proof of devotion, not just feeling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the givers are mostly the leaders listed in 1 Chr 27–28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Guzik: giving came easily once the people saw the value of the project and David's example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: the coin is the Persian daric, which the Jews came to know during the exile. It was not in use in David's time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Gill gives older estimates of what the sums were worth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: Jehiel's family kept the treasury (1 Chr 26:20–22). The scene closely follows the tabernacle offering in Exodus 35. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 9**
- Gill: the people gave cheerfully, not under pressure, and old David rejoiced to see the work so far along. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Guzik and Matthew Henry both link the verse to the "cheerful giver" of 2 Cor 9:7. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 10: a disagreement**
- Guzik (Pentecostal-leaning Calvary Chapel; the label is my description, not from the page): this is the first place in the Bible where God is addressed as **Father**. Jesus may have had the passage in mind when he taught the Lord's Prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Gill disagrees: "our father" refers to Israel (Jacob), not to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Precept Austin says the same. The text calls God the God of the nation's ancestor, while noting that God is our Father (Matt 6:9). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-29-commentary
- The Geneva note reads it as the God who revealed himself to Jacob. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-10.htm
- Pulpit calls verses 10–20 a national liturgy in itself that completely rejects any idea of earning merit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-10.htm
- Gill: David knew God had worked in the people both the will and the act of giving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry: the Lord's Prayer ends with a doxology very like this one ("thine is the kingdom..."). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/29-11.html
- Payne, quoted by Guzik: this verse supplies the ending of the Lord's Prayer (Matt 6:13, KJV). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- The ISBE article on bible.org also links Matt 6:13 to this verse. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=doxology
- Ellicott thinks the word "Thine" may have dropped out before "the kingdom." He explains "the kingdom" as God's universal rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-11.htm
- Clarke quotes the Targum, which expands the verse with God's acts from the Exodus onward. https://www.studylight.org/bible/niv/1-chronicles/29-11.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik: David had plenty of riches and honour, but knew they came from God, not from himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Matthew Henry: David wanted the leaders to see this so they would not think their generosity earned anything from God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_029.cfm
- I found no prosperity-teaching treatment of this verse.

**v. 13**
- Pulpit lists the parts of the prayer: adoration, admitting dependence, humility, dedication, and prayer for the people and for Solomon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-10.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: both the ability to give and the heart to give are gifts from God. Poole, quoted by Guzik, says the same of the riches and the willing heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Sermons on the page argue that we can give God nothing that isn't already his, which rules out merit. Gifts are a trust and we are stewards, not owners. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_chronicles/29-14.htm
- Orthodox: the Divine Liturgy echoes this verse at the offering of the gifts ("Thine own of Thine own, we offer unto Thee"). OCA writers apply it to returning to God what is already his. https://www.oca.org/reflections/berzonsky/thine-own-of-thine-own; https://www.oca.org/wonder/thine-own-of-thine-own-we-offer-unto-thee-offering-ourselves-and-our-lives
- Catholic translations: the Douay-Rheims reads "promise thee all these things," and the NAB "what we give is what we have from you." https://biblehub.com/catholic/1_chronicles/29-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: "without hope" means no lasting future. We are creatures of a day, and our goods are only lent to us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-15.htm
- Several commentators on the same page tie the "strangers" language to Lev 25:23: the land is God's and Israel are his tenants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-15.htm
- Matthew Henry: a short, frail life gives us nothing to boast of before God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_029.cfm
- Guzik: God can take shadow-like pilgrims and use them to build a great house. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Bible Hub's study notes link the verse to Heb 11:13. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/29-15.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik takes vv. 16–19 together as David dedicating the people's offering to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 17**
- Matthew Henry: it comforted David that God, who tests hearts, knew how gladly he gave. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_029.cfm
- Precept Austin connects "test" (bachan) with Prov 17:3 and Job 23:10. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64119/
- Guzik: David gave because he wanted to, not just to set an example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 18: a difference in emphasis**
- Pulpit: the wording echoes Gen 6:5 and 8:21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Matthew Henry: when good takes hold of a heart, we should entrust it to God's grace in prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_029.cfm
- Benson asks God to keep up the grace behind the people's willingness. He adds a prayer that by persevering they "make good our part of the covenant" and do not lose its benefit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-29.html
- Compare Gill on v. 10, who credits the people's willingness entirely to God working in them. The contrast is my own observation: Benson was a Methodist and Gill a Baptist, but neither page presents this as a debate between traditions.

**v. 19**
- Guzik: a loyal heart in Solomon was the key to the kingdom lasting. Morgan, quoted by Guzik, sees the praise turning into prayer for Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Precept Austin notes that Solomon later failed, and the kingdom was divided (1 Kgs 11:11–13). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-29-commentary

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: David receives homage as God's earthly representative. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-20.htm
- Poole and Benson: the Lord received religious worship and the king received civil honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-20.htm
- Matthew Henry: only those who join with lifted hearts share in the blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-20.htm
- Guzik: the people showed their hearts by bowing down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 21**
- Guzik: the day was probably celebrated after David's death. The sacrifices fed the people in a feast before the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 22**
- Guzik: the "second time" was the enthronement after Adonijah's rebellion (1 Kgs 1–2). Trapp, quoted by Guzik, says the first anointing was hasty and this one solemn, but whether it came before or after David's death is uncertain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 23**
- Poole, quoted by Guzik: Israel's throne is "the throne of the Lord" because God gave it, and all kings reign by him (Prov 8:15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/
- Matthew Henry: Solomon's kingdom was a picture of the Messiah's, whose throne is the Lord's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_chronicles/29.htm

**v. 24**
- Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "submitted" is literally "gave the hand under." It may refer to the oath-taking gesture of Gen 24:2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 25**
- Gill: no earlier king, not Saul and not even David, had such majesty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Guzik: Solomon's majesty was inherited from David's work, wisdom, godliness and prayers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**vv. 26–28**
- Precept Austin: David united the twelve tribes. Morgan, quoted there, says Israel's greatness passed its peak when David died. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-29-commentary
- Guzik: David remains Israel's model king, pointing to Jesus, the "Son of David." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-29/

**v. 29**
- Benson and Poole: these sources may be our books of Samuel, written partly by Samuel and continued by Nathan and Gad, or royal annals. Geneva thinks the books of Nathan and Gad were lost in the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-29.htm
- Gill: Scripture preserved what God directed out of these records. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/29.htm
- Pulpit notes that Samuel and Gad are called "seer" with two different Hebrew words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-29.htm

**v. 30**
- Poole and Geneva: "the times" means the changes in David's life, both his troubles and his successes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-30.htm
- A sermon excerpt on the same page (no author given in what I read) says all of life's "times" are meant to bring us nearer to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/29-30.htm
